Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:129: Now a person acquires this whole attribute of humility through the acquisition of holiness — for whoever walks according to the willfulness of his heart after the desires of this world thinks that the whole world is his, and none acquires the attribute of humility except one who is stripped of the affairs of matter and physicality, as explained; for the arrogant one finds the whole world insufficient for the height of his heart. But the discerning person, when he contemplates that all the goods of this world are a passing shadow and a withering flower, that man himself is here today and tomorrow in the grave, and that the soul has no real dwelling in this world at all, and everything is only to prepare for him for his eternal home, he abstains from the desires of this world and draws holiness upon himself in order to cling to his Former, who is the true purpose, for whom the soul awaits its reward, which is to shine with the light of life.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:130: Like the parable of a person whose eye is open, seeing the sweetness of light, and then it happens that he becomes blind — that person forever waits for the time when the veil of blindness will be removed from his eyes through good salves, so that he may return to see the bright light. So the soul, hewn from the light of the supernal life in the supernal world — when the Holy One, blessed be He, imprisoned it in this turbid body, the sight of the supernal luminaries was closed off from it; and the discerning person takes for himself the salve of the holiness of Torah and commandments, and through this his soul is sanctified and clings to the bright light, which is the light of Torah, called "light," as it is written (Proverbs 6:23), "and Torah is light" — and he repents to remove the veil separating him from his God. And although he suffers — for even the blind man suffers when his eyes are salved, whether by a strong ointment or something else — nevertheless he bears it in order to see the light, and sometimes he suffers uncertain whether it will help or not; but one who suffers through repentance surely helps to remove the blindness of his soul, through which it clings to the Creator, and through this the veil of matter is removed from it — for although it remains clothed in matter, the light of the soul increases over the body, and the body no longer becomes a separating veil between him and his God. This is the acquisition of the attributes stated in this passage, up to the attribute of holiness, which is to remove the veil separating the soul until it clings to the Creator; and the other attributes stated — humility, fear, and piety — are all links in a single chain that unfold from holiness, holiness being their father, and humility and the rest being its offspring; for just as one has holiness, humility must necessarily follow, as explained. And with all this, one must give a bond and relation between humility and fear of sin.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:131: When the discerning reader contemplates what we explained in the Gate of Holiness regarding the holiness of each and every limb, he will see that humility must necessarily follow holiness, and they are one bond, brothers who cannot be separated — for if he sanctifies his eyes as stated there, he is lowly-eyed, and this is one of the conditions of humility. And if he sanctifies his tongue as stated there, he surely will not utter insults in the manner of one who is angry. And if he sanctifies his heart, he must distance from it jealousy and hatred, and he is thereby humble. It follows that all the conditions and particulars of humility depend on a person's sanctifying himself properly, as we explained there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:132: It is also possible to give another bond and relation between holiness and humility, and through it the reason and bond of humility with fear of sin may be understood. The matter is that the essence of holiness depends on the holiness of thought, as explained in the Zohar (parashat Vayetze 155a), which we quoted in the Gate of Holiness — that regarding the holiness of thought it is said (Leviticus 20:7), "and you shall sanctify yourselves and be holy" — and holiness of thought can come only through the soul, as we elaborated at length in the Gate of Holiness, chapter 4.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:133: In the Zohar (parashat Tetzaveh 182a), in the explanation of the verse (Isaiah 2:22), "cease from man, in whose nostrils is a soul [neshamah]" — it says there that when a person becomes angry, the soul departs from him; and not only the neshamah, but even the nefesh, as it is written (Job 18:4), "who tears his soul [nafsho] in his anger." With this, the precision of his language there may be understood, where he says, "and his soul is a holy spirit, comprising three" — as we have established, that there is nefesh, ru'ach, and neshamah. And he further says afterward, that these three powers are all one. This whole introduction is to reconcile the verses, since one verse says "tears his soul in his anger," and another verse says "in whose nostrils is a soul [neshamah]" — and for this he prefaced by saying that all three are one bond, and all depart, and the blemish is in all of them.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:134: So too he says afterward, "and not only that, but the supernal holiness is uprooted from its place, and a strange god comes to dwell in its place." It appears that the whole reality of holiness — from nefesh, ru'ach, and neshamah — all departs, and a strange god rests there instead. He further says, "and whoever converses with him is as one who has literally joined idolatry" — and if any spirit or soul had remained, it would not have been literal idolatry, since some holiness would still be in him; rather, surely everything departs.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:135: We are compelled to say that this blemish reaching nefesh, ru'ach, and neshamah does not refer to the nefesh, ru'ach, and neshamah of Atzilut, but rather the nefesh, ru'ach, and neshamah of the category of Chayah and Kise [i.e., the lower configurations] — that the blemish actually damages them, for the intent is not merely departure but that they are actually blemished, as our sages, of blessed memory, said: and if that holy soul is brought into another service, this defiles it and it departs from the service of its Master. And so it further says there, that that holy soul is torn and defiled because of his anger, etc. But regarding the soul of Atzilut, we cannot speak of impurity and blemish in it, as explained in the Tikkunim (98b), in these words: there is an "Adam" who is an angel, and this is Metatron; and there is an "Adam" in the pattern of the Holy One, blessed be He, which is His Atzilut, and this is Yod-Heh, Vav-Heh, and he has no Beriah, Yetzirah, and Asiyah, but only Atzilut, and in this place there is no sin and no death — this being what is written (Psalms 5:5), "evil shall not sojourn with You." — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:136: If a blemish is found in one who has a soul of Atzilut, it is explained in the Tikkunim (124a) that the intent is not an actual blemish, that its light be darkened, but rather departure of the soul of Atzilut is the blemish that reaches it — and we quoted this passage in the Gate of Fear, chapter 9; see there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:137: Now, based on these introductions from the words of the Rashbi, peace be upon him, we may say that what the passage says, "holiness leads to humility," is this: whoever merits a soul of Atzilut, which is surely holy, as we quoted the Rashbi's statement, peace be upon him, in the Gate of Holiness, chapter 4, will merit humility, so that he not come to anger, thereby blemishing his soul — for that supernal holy soul is not given to one who would blemish it, at every moment it might depart from him — for one who is angry and has that evil trait becomes angry over a trivial matter; rather, surely, having already merited a soul of Atzilut, which is holy, this will bring him to humility, so that his inclination be subdued, so that holiness not be lost from him, and it will be fulfilled in him (Proverbs 12:28), "no harm shall befall the righteous." And one who has not merited the holy soul, in whom the outside force still has some grip, this too will bring him to anger, so that a strange god rests within him, because he has not been properly purified from his sins. Therefore he must strive to attain the attribute of humility together with all the attributes mentioned, until he attains holiness — and since he is holy and the impure outside force has no share in him, surely he will not defile himself with anger, which defiles him both within and without, as explained there in parashat Tetzaveh.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:138: Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, because of the merit of his supernal soul, possessed great humility — "and the man Moses was very humble, more than all men," etc. (Numbers 12:3) — and yet, nevertheless, it is said of him (Numbers 31:14), "and Moses was angry," etc., and our sages, of blessed memory, explained (Vayikra Rabbah 13:1) that a halachah was hidden from him — for according to the fineness and purity of his soul, even a small matter would blemish him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:139: By this we may understand what is said, "humility leads to fear of sin" — for fear of sin means that he fears lest even a small sin come into his hand, for according to what supernal soul he has merited, so must he fear sin. The parable for this: an oil stain falling on garments — a stain falling on a linen garment is not equal to a stain falling on a fine woolen garment, nor to one falling on silk and embroidered garments. So the reality of blemish is not equal for one who has a nefesh, one who has a ru'ach, and one who has a neshamah — this being what our sages, of blessed memory, explained (Yevamot 121b) on "and all around Him it storms greatly" (Psalms 50:3): the Holy One, blessed be He, is exacting with the righteous to the width of a hair's breadth — for a hair's breadth is a great blemish relative to the fineness of their souls, like a great sin, comparable to a wagon-rope's thickness, for the rest of the people.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:140: Perhaps for this reason Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai trembled at the time of his death (Berachot 28b), saying, I do not know which way I am being led — for according to his wisdom he surely merited a supernal soul, and even a small blemish would be considered great.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:141: Whoever merits humility will merit fear of sin, and it follows of itself — for just as he is guarded against anger so that his soul not depart from him, and cause "one sin destroys much good" (Ecclesiastes 9:18) — for they said in parashat Tetzaveh that after a person sins through anger, would that he be [re]sanctified, since a strange god rests in his body and does not depart easily — therefore he must fear sin, that he not blemish himself again, even with a small sin, so as not to lose the rank of his soul — for the blemish may at times cause the holy spiritual soul to depart and never return, and it is a loss that does not come back, and it will require many preparations before it returns to what it was, would that it should return.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:142: According to the approaches I explained above regarding "holiness leads to humility," by these same approaches the matter of fear of sin may also be reconciled — for one who sins literally before the king is not comparable to one who sins in his courtyard, or in his province; so too one who draws near to the Holy One, blessed be He, through his good deeds, and thinks that he always stands before Him, and because of this has humility, as explained — for this same reason he will fear sin, even a small sin, for he would be ashamed to sin before the King before whom he stands, since it is not fitting to provoke the King in any small or great matter.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:143: "Fear of sin leads to," etc. — everything we have intended to explain in this baraita is to explain the attribute of piety, for it is the acquisition of the attribute of love, as it is written (Psalms 31:24), "love the Lord, all His pious ones" — for whoever reaches the rank called "chasid" is a lover, and the holy spirit rests upon him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:144: Now, the attribute of piety in general is that one conduct himself in all his affairs beyond the letter of the law, as it says in the Gemara (see Yerushalmi ch. 8, halachah 4), "is this not the teaching of the pious? For one must act beyond the letter of the law." This attribute is one of the attributes, blessed be He, by which He conducts Himself with His creatures, as it is written (Micah 7:18), "for He delights in kindness," and likewise (Exodus 34:7), "who keeps kindness for thousands," and "abundant in kindness" (ibid. 34:6), and many similar verses.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:145: After a person is complete in fear, so that he does not sin even a small sin, he is exempted from the attribute of judgment and the attribute of Chesed rests upon him. The reason is that when a person sins even slightly, of necessity the attribute of judgment must accompany him to purify and discipline him from that blemish, and once the judgment is completed upon him, then Chesed receives him. This is the reason Michael brings the souls of the righteous near (Zohar, parashat Lech Lecha 80a; Tosafot, Menachot 110a), for the right is what brings near after the souls are purified from the River of Fire (Zohar, parashat Pekudei 211a).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:146: Now, the attribute of Chesed has branches that one who wishes to merit it must hold fast to, and the branches of Chesed are explained in Scripture. The first attribute one must hold fast to, of Chesed, is the Torah, which is drawn from it, as it is said (Proverbs 31:26), "and the Torah of kindness is on her tongue," and as our sages, of blessed memory, said (Avot 2:5), "an ignorant person cannot be pious" — and it is explained in Ra'aya Meheimna (parashat Tzav 33a) with a sweet teaching on this matter, saying that Torah is drawn from Chochmah, which is Yod, and the chasid is called Chesed when he brings the Yod, which is Chochmah, into it — this is Chesed-Yod; and the ignorant person [am ha'aretz], who has not merited Torah, has not merited Chochmah, and therefore it is not fitting for him to be called chasid, for he lacks the Yod.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:147: Further, in order to merit, one must engage in Torah from midnight onward until the light of morning, in order to receive the thread of Chesed drawn from Chesed upon the Shechinah, and upon those who engage in Torah who have grasped it, as elaborated at length in the Zohar in several places, particularly in parashat Vayikra (21b); this is what our sages, of blessed memory, said (Chagigah 12b), whoever engages in Torah at night, a thread of Chesed is drawn upon him by day — and "night" here refers to after midnight, for before midnight it is called "eve," as explained in the Tikkunim (20).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:148: Further, among the attributes of Chesed is holding fast to charity and acts of lovingkindness in all their particulars, as will be explained in its place, with God's help — for all these are branches of Chesed.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:149: Further, one must fast if he has the strength for it, as they said in Ta'anit (11a-b): if he can afflict himself, he is called holy; if not, he is called a sinner. And if he can afflict himself he is called both holy and pious, as it is written (Proverbs 11:17), "the pious man rewards [gomel] his own soul." And so our sages, of blessed memory, said (Ta'anit, ibid.), in these words: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said, whoever sits in a fast is called pious, as it is said, "the pious man rewards [gomel] his own soul." And Rashi, peace be upon him, explained "gomel nafsho" — that he separates his soul from food and drink, as in "on the day Isaac was weaned [higamel]" — from the mouth of my master. Alternatively, "gomel" is a term for reward [tagmul], that he completes his soul to his Creator.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:150: The reason he is called a man of chesed may be explained by what is explained in the Zohar (parashat Shemot 20b), that this is the image of a rose, which is red and white, and when it is squeezed by fire, everything turns white, for the liquid that comes out is white. So one who sits in a fast and diminishes his fat and blood, and fire overpowers him — the aroma rising from his mouth is like the aroma of the sacrifice, which shrank due to the fire and turned white, and he is atoned for. It follows from this that he is called by [the attribute of] chesed, which is whiteness.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:151: Surely, Reish Lakish's words are said only regarding one who has sinned and must return in repentance — for if he fasts, he is called a man of chesed. The reason is that since he sinned through the sustenance that flowed to him from the side of Chesed, he must reward his soul from that sustenance, from eating and drinking, and thereby repay it measure for measure — for through what she sinned she shall be struck — for a person sins only through eating and drinking, as explained in the Gate of Holiness. But a Torah scholar who has not sinned need not fast — proof from Hillel the Elder, as we shall quote below — for since he was pious, and in all his days never grew angry, he would eat in order to reward himself with kindness.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:152: Further, Reish Lakish himself said there that a Torah scholar is not permitted to fast, in these words: Rabbi Yirmeyah bar Abba said in the name of Reish Lakish, a Torah scholar is not permitted to sit in a fast, because he thereby diminishes the work of Heaven. — end of quotation. Rashi, peace be upon him, explained "diminishes the work of Heaven" — he becomes weak and cannot study.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:153: In our own time, no Torah scholar is free of sin, particularly of slander or other categories that do not receive the countenance of the Shechinah, and therefore it is fitting that he fast. And if you say that Torah atones for sin, I answer you from David the king, peace be upon him, who was a Torah scholar, head of the Sanhedrin, and yet all his days were in fasting after he sinned, as we shall explain in the Gate of Repentance (chapter 3).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:154: Further, it is possible to give another reason why it is fitting that one who fasts be called a chasid: because one who eats is sustained according to the nature of the world, like the other creatures who eat to sustain their bodies, and the world was created according to nature, which is Elohim — for "teva" [nature] has the same numerical value as "Elohim" — and therefore the world was created with Elohim, "In the beginning God [Elohim] created" (Genesis 1:1), and the word "Elohim" is mentioned thirty-two times there, and all things follow nature, such as oil that kindles and water that extinguishes fire — this is according to nature. Now, the pious one overturns nature and says, He who told oil to kindle can tell vinegar to kindle (Ta'anit 25a). In this manner, one who fasts, not wishing to conduct himself according to nature like the rest of the creatures, surely his sustenance is according to Chesed, which is fine, spiritual sustenance, in the manner of the sustenance of Torah scholars, whose sustenance is the sustenance of the soul flowing from Chochmah, as explained in the Gate of Holiness. Therefore it is fitting that he be called chasid, Chesed-Yod, for the Yod partners with Chesed to sustain the pious ones who hold fast to the Name.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:155: So too you find that the angels are sustained from the side of Chesed, as explained in the Zohar (parashat Vayera 104a). Therefore souls in the World to Come are sustained from the side of Chesed, for the soul is called "a priest's daughter," as explained in the Zohar (parashat Mishpatim 95a-b), where it is written (Leviticus 22:12), "and if a priest's daughter is married to a strange man, she shall not eat of the terumah of the holy things" — implying that if she was not married to a strange man, referring to the evil inclination, she eats of the terumah of the holy things, flowing from Chesed, for all holiness is from the side of the right Yod. Likewise, "but she shall eat of her father's bread" indicates this; and so in the Zohar (parashat Terumah 166b), regarding "to cause those who love me to inherit substance"; see there. A sign of this matter is (Psalms 62:13), "and to You, O Lord, is kindness, for You repay each man," etc.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:156: In any case, if he needs to eat or bathe in the bathhouse for the health of his body, he too is called "the pious man rewards his own soul," as in the story of Hillel the Elder, peace be upon him, brought in Vayikra Rabbah (34:3) on the verse "if your brother becomes poor" (Leviticus 25:39), in these words: "the pious man rewards his own soul" — this is Hillel the Elder, who, when he took leave of his students, would walk along with them. They said to him, where are you going? He said to them, to perform a commandment. They said to him, what commandment is Hillel performing? He said to them, to bathe in the bathhouse. They said to him, is this a commandment? He said to them, yes — for if the statues of kings, set up in circuses and theaters, are washed and scrubbed by their appointed caretaker, and they raise garments for him [as reward], and moreover he is elevated by royal favors — we, who were created in the image and likeness [of God], as it is written (Genesis 9:6), "for in the image of God He made man," how much more so! And likewise, Hillel the Elder used to say to his students, at the time he took leave of them: I am going to perform kindness with this guest who is in the house. They said to him, do you have guests every day? He said to them, is this poor soul not a guest within the body — here today and tomorrow gone? Another interpretation, "the pious man rewards his own soul" — one who distributes charitable gifts [mitzvot]. "But he who is cruel troubles his own flesh [she'ero]" — Rabbi Alexandri said, this refers to one who has an occasion of joy and does not draw his relatives close to him because of their poverty; therefore Moses warns Israel, "you shall surely give to him." — end of quotation. He explained "distributes charitable gifts" [mitzvot] as giving charity, and this is evident in Vayikra Rabbah.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:157: Further, one who holds fast to the attribute of Chesed is one who hears his own insult and is silent, as our sages, of blessed memory, said (Yalkut, Tehillim, remez 669) on the verse (Psalms 16:10), "You will not give Your pious one to see corruption" — in these words: the Holy One, blessed be He, is called "chasid," as it is said (Jeremiah 3:12), "for I am chasid, says the Lord"; and David called himself chasid, as it is said (Psalms 86:2), "guard my soul, for I am chasid." "You will not give Your pious one to see corruption" — Rav Huna said in the name of Rabbi Alexandri, whoever hears his own curse and is silent is called a chasid, and David heard his own curse and was silent.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:158: This attribute is one of the attributes of the lover, as our sages, of blessed memory, expounded (Shabbat 88b) on the verse (Judges 5:31), "and let those who love Him be as the sun going forth in its strength" — our rabbis taught: those who are insulted but do not insult, who hear their own disgrace and do not respond, who act out of love and rejoice in suffering — of them Scripture says, "and let those who love Him be as the sun going forth in its strength." — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:159: Likewise, among the attributes of Chesed is that he not bear a grudge, hold enmity, or become angry — as the prophet Jeremiah said (Jeremiah 3:12), "return, backsliding Israel, says the Lord, I will not cause My anger to fall upon you, for I am chasid, says the Lord, I will not bear a grudge forever."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:160: The rule is: since a person exempts himself from the attributes of judgment and cruelty, and deals with people beyond the letter of the law, he merits the attribute of Chesed — for by strict judgment and standing without love, it would be fitting for him to respond to his own insult and become angry at whoever damaged his honor; but one who forgives merits Chesed, just as the Holy One, blessed be He, deals with His creatures through the attribute of Chesed, as it is said (Psalms 103:10), "He has not dealt with us according to our sins."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:161: Of this the Zohar says (parashat Naso 145a): we have learned, any person who possesses piety is called an angel of the Lord of hosts — this is what is written (Malachi 2:7), "for the priest's lips shall guard knowledge, and they shall seek Torah from his mouth, for he is an angel of the Lord of hosts." And it says, that just as Michael is a priest above and is from the side of Chesed, so the priest, from the side of Chesed, is an angel of the Lord below; and the person who possesses piety enters beyond the letter of the law with everyone, and it follows that he does not conduct himself according to the nature of this world, which was created according to the letter of the law, but rather according to the World to Come, which was created with the Yod (Menachot 29b) — that is, the right, Chochmah, the root of Chesed (Ra'aya Meheimna, parashat Pinchas 227b); and therefore piety is greater than all the rest.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:162: On the verse "guard my soul, for I am chasid" (Psalms 86:2), this matter is brought (Yalkut, ibid., remez 834), and in another version: whoever hears his own disgrace and has it within his power to protest but is silent is called chasid — and this version appears more correct.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:163: Further, our sages, of blessed memory, said (Berachot 4a): Rabbi Levi and Rabbi Yitzchak — one said, David said this before the Holy One, blessed be He: Master of the universe, am I not pious, that all the kings of east and west sleep until the third hour of the day, while I rise at midnight to thank You? And the other said, David said this before the Holy One, blessed be He: Master of the universe, am I not pious, that all the kings of east and west sit in groups in their honor before them, while my hands are soiled with the blood of the fetus and the placenta, in order to purify a woman for her husband? And not only that, but everything I do, I consult with Mephivoshet my teacher, and I say to him, Mephivoshet my teacher, have I judged rightly, have I condemned rightly, have I acquitted rightly, have I declared impure rightly, have I declared pure rightly? — and I was not ashamed. Rabbi Yehoshua the son of Rav Idi said, what is the verse [for this]? (Psalms 119:46), "and I shall speak of Your testimonies before kings, and shall not be ashamed." — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:164: We learn from this passage that one who rises at midnight is called chasid. And likewise, one who diminishes himself before one greater than himself and is not ashamed to ask him a matter of Torah law is called chasid. And the verse Rabbi Yehoshua brought, "and I shall speak of Your testimonies before kings," we must interpret "kings" here as referring to the sages, as they said (Gittin 62a), who are the "kings" [of Psalms]? These are the rabbis. In general, we learn from this passage that whoever does something not strictly obligated of him by Torah law is called chasid in these matters mentioned in the passage — to purify a woman for her husband, and the rest.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:165: Further, among the branches of Chesed is that one rebuke his fellow — and this is an act of kindness [gemilut chasadim], for he thereby performs kindness with that soul; and one who is rebuked should accept his fellow's rebuke for the sake of Heaven, and consider that rebuke a kindness done to him, for through it he is saved from the judgment of Gehinnom, as David the king, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 141:5), "let the righteous strike me in kindness and rebuke me." On the matter of rebuke we have elaborated at length in the Gate of Humility, chapter 5.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:166: Further, among the branches of Chesed is one who trusts in the Lord, as it is said (Psalms 32:10), "but he who trusts in the Lord, kindness shall surround him." And they said in Midrash Vayikra Rabbah, Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Tanchum: even a wicked person, if he trusts in the Lord, kindness shall surround him. — end of quotation. The intent being that they expounded the juxtaposition of the verse "many are the sorrows of the wicked, but he who trusts," etc.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:167: Further, our sages, of blessed memory, said (Bava Kama 30a): whoever wishes to be pious should fulfill the matters of Berachot, the matters of Nezikin, and the matters of Avot. — end of quotation. The reason for the matters of Berachot is that he thereby has a good eye and is blessed, as explained above. Likewise the matters of Nezikin — for one who damages his fellow becomes a portion of judgment from Gevurah, to punish his fellow, and he is thereby distanced from Chesed, which benefits all; therefore he must study the laws of damages so as not to come to damage his fellow. And the matters of Avot is self-evident.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:168: Further, in order to merit Chesed, one must be a God-fearing person, as it is said (Psalms 103:17), "but the kindness of the Lord is from everlasting to everlasting upon those who fear Him" — for the ascent of the grades from below upward is first through fear and afterward through Chesed. Behold, the Shechinah is called "fear" (Ra'aya Meheimna, parashat Pinchas 229b); one must hold fast to the particulars of fear within it, and afterward ascend to the male world, which is Chesed, for the Righteous One [Tzaddik/Yesod] is called Chesed, as explained in the Idra of Naso (142a). Likewise Chesed-Gevurah: Gevurah is called fear — one must be careful regarding the negative commandments — and afterward he shall merit Chesed, which is the fulfillment of the positive commandments; and the particulars of fear are the attributes mentioned — alacrity, cleanliness, purity — and further particulars will be explained in the Gate of Holiness; and all the attributes we explained in this Gate are the grades that lead to becoming a chasid.
